content: MT-TP, also known as mitochondrially encoded tRNA proline, is a transfer RNA molecule encoded by the mitochondrial MT-TP gene in humans. The MT-TP gene is located on the p arm of mitochondrial DNA at position 12 and spans 68 base pairs. The structure of a tRNA molecule is characterized by a distinctive folded shape, which includes three hairpin loops and resembles a three-leafed clover. MT-TP is a small RNA molecule consisting of 68 nucleotides (mapped to human mitochondrial DNA positions 15956–16023). It plays a critical role in protein synthesis by transferring the amino acid proline to a growing polypeptide chain at the ribosome during translation. Additionally, MT-TP is involved in coding for the microsomal triglyceride transfer protein, which is essential for the synthesis of beta-lipoproteins in the liver and intestine. Beta-lipoproteins are crucial for the transport of fats, cholesterol, and fat-soluble vitamins from the intestine to the bloodstream for absorption. Mutations in the MT-TP gene have been linked to abetalipoproteinemia, a rare inherited disorder characterized by impaired absorption of dietary fats and certain vitamins. These mutations disrupt the function of the microsomal triglyceride transfer protein, leading to reduced or absent beta-lipoproteins. As a result, there are insufficient levels of fats, cholesterol, and vitamins necessary for growth and development. Clinical manifestations of abetalipoproteinemia include poor weight gain, growth failure, diarrhea, and steatorrhea. Specific mutations in the MT-TP gene associated with this condition include GLY865TER, SER590ILE, ASN780TYR, ARG540HIS, IVS9AS, and ARG215TER. MT-TP mutations can also result in complex I deficiency of the mitochondrial respiratory chain. This condition can present with a wide range of symptoms affecting multiple organ systems, particularly the nervous system, heart, and skeletal muscles. Symptoms may appear at any age, from birth to adulthood, and include encephalopathy, epilepsy, dystonia, hypotonia, myalgia, exercise intolerance, and more. A G15975A mutation has been identified in a patient with complex I deficiency. Furthermore, MT-TP mutations have been associated with late-onset ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa, deafness, leukoencephalopathy, and complex IV deficiency.
